title: How to Get Through Your Curriculum This Year (Credibility Booster)
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Written as a Credibility booster, this short guide addresses the perennial teacher problem of running out of time to finish the curriculum. Stuart argues that chronically falling behind schedule quietly undermines Teacher Credibility, and offers two concrete time-management tools: using a stopwatch to enforce Gentle Urgency at the lesson level, and building a calendar of predetermined assessment dates to keep units, and the semester, on pace. He frames both tools as balancing two competing realities of classroom time: the human variability of students and lessons, and the reality that deadlines produce solutions. Only after using both tools consistently, he argues, can a teacher fairly conclude that a bloated curriculum, rather than their own practice, is the real bottleneck.
points: Stuart connects curriculum pacing directly to Credibility, arguing that habitually rushing or skipping the final unit undermines the belief that is both the most fundamental and the most controllable of the Five Key Beliefs.
His stopwatch tool isn't about maniacal time pressure, it's Gentle Urgency, balancing compassion for how humans vary in pace against the reality that deadlines produce solutions.
Setting predetermined assessment dates on a calendar before the year starts lets him make ongoing mid-unit adjustments rather than discovering a pacing shortfall in week 30.
He explicitly withholds sympathy for blaming a bad curriculum until a teacher has consistently used both tools, arguing it's more honest to examine one's own time-management practice first.
quotes: Schedules get disrupted, tangents get taken, rants get ranted, projects go over, and deadlines get shifted. Before you know it, you're weeks behind where you need to be to finish the curriculum.
And I'd also argue that it undermines our Credibility, which is both the most fundamental and the most controllable of the student motivation beliefs that exist in our classrooms.
Give me no deadline, and I'll write you a book when I get to it. Give me deadlines, and I may miss the first few, but I'll get that book out way before I would have had I not had any deadlines.
This helps me make mid-unit adjustments, like: Where can I speed things up if I'm short on time? Where can I linger if we've got extra time I hadn't planned on?
Now you'll know that you're not the problem, the curriculum is. And you can make or advocate for the adjustments that need to happen.
But until you use these two tools, I don't think it's accurate to point the finger at the curriculum.
